newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU details probe on Banco di Napoli plan.
newsitem.headline: EU details probe on Banco di Napoli plan.

text.p: The European Commission published on Tuesday a long list of questions regarding the rescue of Banco di Napoli, one of Italy's top ten banks which faces serious liquidity problems after a reckless expansion in the early 1990s.

The European Union's competition watchdog particularly requested Italy to submit a detailed recovery programme for the Banco di Napoli group, including estimates for the next four years, and information on the arrangements and timing of the capital increases and other support planned for the bank.

In July, the Commission started a formal probe into a proposed 2.0 billion lire capital injection into the bank by the Italian Treasury as well as advances made by the Italian central bank and tax concessions.
The list of the documents requested by the Commission in a notice published in the Official Journal of November 1 include:

- a note detailing the restructuring measures planned for the bank focusing in particular on the restructuring of the credit management services, investment and risk control services, the measures for reducing staff expenditure and the rationalisation of the agency network;
- analysis and assessments carried out by Rothschild and other consultants to the Italian Treasury or Banco di Napoli itself;
- a note on the position and economic prospects of the bank's subsidiaries abroad;
- and whether compensation has been offered to competitors to offset the distortion of competition caused by the aid.

It its preliminary assessment, the Commission found that the rescue plan harmed competition not only in Italy but in the Union as a whole since there are no barriers to the provision of financial services in the 15-nation bloc.

"Aid aimed at enabling even local banks to survive which would otherwise have been forced out of the market owing to their lower profitability and competitive capacity is liable to distort compertition...as it makes it more difficult for foreign banks to enter the Italian market", the notice said.
"Without the aid in question, the bank would probably have been wound up or sold to another more solid financial institution", it added.
The Commission gave national governments and other interested parties time to comment on the restructuring of Napoli within a month.

In 1995, it approved a 45-billion-franc ($8.8 billion) rescue plan for France's Credit Lyonnais and is expected to receive shortly a fresh French request to inject more public money in the troubled bank. -- Brussels newsroom 322 2876841 ($ = 5.108 French Francs)
